quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten quick checks on what warp rib, weft rib, hopsack and basket weaves are and how they grow out of plain weave.

questions.q: A warp rib is produced from plain weave by doing what to the interlacing?
options: Extending it weft-way so every pick covers two ends
Extending it warp-way so every end moves over two picks at a time
Extending it both ways so pairs of ends and pairs of picks work as one
Shifting every second end by one pick
questions.explain: In a warp rib each end lifts over two picks and then sinks under two; the interlacing is stretched warp-way. Extending it weft-way (every pick over two ends) gives a weft rib, and both ways gives a hopsack.

questions.q: In which direction do the ridges (cords) of a warp rib run?
options: Warp-way, along the length of the cloth
Weft-way, across the width of the cloth
They do not form visible ridges
questions.explain: The lecture states that in a warp rib the ridges run weft-way. The warp bends over pairs of picks, so each pair of picks forms a cord across the cloth; a warp-way cord would belong to a weft rib.

questions.q: In a warp rib the weft is hidden and the warp crimp is high.
questions.explain: The warp does all the bending: each end passes over and under two picks at a time, so it takes up heavily (high warp crimp) and covers the weft, which lies almost straight and out of sight.

questions.q: Which weave has pairs of ends and pairs of picks interlacing as if each pair were a single thread?
questions.explain: Hopsack extends the plain interlacing both ways: two ends work together over two picks, and two picks together over two ends. A rib extends only one way; a 2/2 twill moves each end one pick along and so forms a diagonal.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT another name for the hopsack weave?
questions.explain: Matt, panama and basket are all names used for hopsack. Herringbone is a twill derivative in which the twill line is reversed and cut — a different family entirely.

questions.q: Rib and hopsack weaves are reversible because their floats show equally on both sides of the cloth.
questions.explain: Each thread floats over two and under two, so what shows on the face shows equally on the back. That is why the lecture calls these weaves reversible, unlike a warp-faced satin.

questions.q: The fancy basket 3-2 shown in the lecture is formed from which arrangement of threads?
options: Groups of three ends and three picks
Unequal groups of three and two threads
Single ends with pairs of picks
Groups of two ends with single picks
questions.explain: The 3-2 basket uses unequal groups — three threads then two — which gives the irregular basket texture used in shirtings and upholstery. Equal groups of three would simply be a 3/3 hopsack.

questions.q: A 2/2 weft rib results when which of these happens to plain weave?
options: Every end lifts over two picks
Every end and every pick cover two threads
Every end is drawn on its own heald
questions.explain: In a weft rib the ends work in pairs, so every pick passes over two ends and under two. Each end still rises and falls on every pick, as in plain weave; it is the pick that floats.

questions.q: Compared with plain weave, how often do rib and hopsack weaves interlace, and what does that mean for the sett?
options: More often, so they can be set more openly
Less often, so they need a higher sett to look firm
Exactly as often, so the sett is unchanged
Less often, so they need a lower sett
questions.explain: Threads that float over two instead of one interlace half as often, so the cloth is looser at the same sett. The lecture therefore says ribs and hopsacks need a higher sett than plain weave to look firm, not a lower one.

questions.q: Which weave hides the weft yarn almost completely under the warp?
questions.explain: In a warp rib the warp bends over pairs of picks and covers them, so the weft is hidden. In a weft rib the roles are reversed and the weft is prominent; hopsack and basket show both sets of threads equally.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: Repeat sizes, heald counts, cover-factor divisors and what changes when the floats get longer.

questions.q: What is the repeat of a 2/2 warp rib?
questions.explain: Each end lifts for two picks and sinks for two, so four picks complete the cycle, while only two ends (one up, one down) are needed across. Four ends × two picks is the weft rib.

questions.q: What is the repeat of a 2/2 weft rib?
questions.explain: Ends work in pairs, so a pair up and a pair down take four ends; each end alternates every pick, so two picks complete the repeat. Two ends × four picks is the warp rib.

questions.q: Which cover-factor divisor does the lecture give for a warp rib?
questions.explain: The divisors quoted are 1.26 for warp rib, 1.5 for weft rib and 1.4 for panama (hopsack). A divisor of 1.0 would be plain weave itself.

questions.q: Which of these weaves has the largest cover-factor divisor in the lecture's list?
questions.explain: Weft rib has the largest divisor, 1.5, against 1.4 for panama and 1.26 for warp rib. Plain weave is the reference and has no divisor applied.

questions.q: The divisor for panama (1.4) lies between the divisors for warp rib and weft rib.
questions.explain: Warp rib 1.26 < panama 1.4 < weft rib 1.5, so the hopsack sits between the two ribs.

questions.q: What is the minimum number of healds needed to weave a 2/2 warp rib?
questions.explain: There are only two different end movements — odd ends and even ends work opposite to each other — so two healds suffice, exactly as the lecture states. Four healds would be chosen only to spread the ends, not because the weave needs them.

questions.q: When plain weave is changed into a warp rib with the same yarns, what happens to the warp crimp?
options: It becomes equal to the weft crimp
questions.explain: The warp now bends over and under pairs of picks, which are thicker together than a single pick, so the warp takes up more — warp crimp is high in a warp rib, as the lecture notes. The weft lies straighter, so the crimps are far from equal.

questions.q: If a 2/2 hopsack is woven at exactly the same sett as a plain weave in the same yarns, how will it compare?
questions.explain: The hopsack interlaces half as often, so with the same threads per inch it is a looser, flatter cloth — the lecture's own description. Weight per square metre hardly changes because the same yarns are present.

questions.q: Going from a 2/2 hopsack to a 3/3 hopsack, how do the float length and the repeat change?
questions.explain: In a 3/3 hopsack each thread floats over three and under three, so the repeat is 3 + 3 = 6 ends × 6 picks. Nine would be the square of the group size, which is a common slip.

questions.q: In a 2/2 weft rib each end floats over two picks before interlacing.
questions.explain: In a weft rib it is the pick that floats over two ends; every end still goes over one pick and under the next, just as in plain weave. Warp floats of two picks belong to the warp rib.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Counting repeats, floats, lifts and healds on the point paper, plus a cover-factor adjustment.

questions.q: A 2/2 warp rib repeats on 2 ends × 4 picks. How many repeats of the weave fit across a warp of 48 ends?
questions.explain: Repeats across = ends ÷ ends per repeat = 48 ÷ 2 = 24.

questions.q: A 2/2 weft rib repeats on 4 ends × 2 picks. How many repeats of the weave are completed in 60 picks?
questions.explain: Repeats weft-way = picks ÷ picks per repeat = 60 ÷ 2 = 30.

questions.q: A 3/3 hopsack repeats on 6 ends × 6 picks. How many squares of point paper does one repeat occupy?
questions.explain: One repeat covers 6 × 6 = 36 squares.

questions.q: The lecture draws the 2/2 hopsack on 8 ends × 8 picks (two repeats each way). How many squares are filled (end up) in that drawing?
questions.explain: Every end is up for half the picks (two up, two down), so half of the 64 squares are filled: 64 ÷ 2 = 32.

questions.q: In a 3/3 hopsack, over how many picks does the longest warp float pass?
questions.explain: A 3/3 hopsack lifts each end over three picks and drops it under three, so the longest float is three picks.

questions.q: In the fancy basket 3-2, groups of three and two threads alternate. How many ends does one group of three plus one group of two cover?
questions.explain: One cycle of the unequal grouping is 3 + 2 = 5 ends.

questions.q: In a 2/2 hopsack each end interlaces once every two picks. How many times does one end interlace in 12 picks?
questions.explain: 12 picks ÷ 2 picks per interlacing = 6 interlacings. A plain-weave end would interlace 12 times in the same picks.

questions.q: Treat the plain-weave equivalent cover factor as the weave's cover factor divided by its divisor. A warp rib is woven at a warp cover factor of 25.2; using the divisor 1.26, what is the plain-weave equivalent? Give it to one decimal.
questions.explain: 25.2 ÷ 1.26 = 20.0. The rib set at 25.2 is only as firm as a plain weave at 20.

questions.q: How many healds, at minimum, does a 3/3 hopsack need?
questions.explain: The three ends of a group all move identically, and the other group moves opposite, so there are only two different end movements and two healds suffice. Six is the repeat width, not the heald count.

questions.q: In the 8 × 8 point-paper drawing of the 2/2 warp rib, on how many of the 8 picks is end 1 lifted?
questions.explain: End 1 lifts for two picks and sinks for two, so in 8 picks it is up on 4 picks and down on 4.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Choosing between ribs, hopsacks and baskets on the mill floor and avoiding the usual mistakes with sett.

questions.q: A buyer wants a cloth with prominent cords running across the width and the weft completely covered. Which weave should the designer choose?
questions.explain: Warp rib gives ridges running weft-way with the weft hidden under the high-crimp warp. A weft rib would show the weft and run its cords the other way.

questions.q: A 2/2 hopsack sample woven at the mill's standard plain-weave sett looks sleazy and open. What is the correct fix?
options: Raise the ends and picks per inch
questions.explain: Hopsack interlaces half as often as plain weave and needs a higher sett to look firm. Going to 3/3 lengthens the floats and makes the cloth looser still.

questions.q: A shirting customer asks for an irregular basket look rather than a plain regular matt. Which weave fits?
questions.explain: The fancy basket with unequal groups of three and two gives the irregular basket texture the lecture mentions for shirtings and upholstery; regular hopsacks are even and symmetrical.

questions.q: Because a warp rib is reversible, the weaver must take special care to keep the face side up during finishing.
questions.explain: Reversible means the floats show equally on both sides, so there is no distinct face and back to worry about. The statement contradicts itself.

questions.q: A warp rib quality uses noticeably more warp yarn per metre of cloth than the plain weave it replaced. What is the main reason?
options: The warp rib needs twice as many ends
Warp crimp is high because the ends bend over pairs of picks
The weft is heavier in a warp rib
questions.explain: Warp take-up (crimp) is high in a warp rib, so more warp length goes into each metre of cloth. The number of ends is set by the sett, not by the weave itself.

questions.q: Using the lecture's divisors, which weave would need the greatest increase in sett over plain weave to reach the same firmness?
options: They all need the same increase
questions.explain: The larger the divisor, the more the cover factor must be raised to match plain weave; weft rib's 1.5 is the largest of the three.

questions.q: On point paper a designer draws every end going over two picks and under two, while every pick goes over one end and under one. Which weave has been drawn?
questions.explain: Warp floats of two picks with the weft interlacing singly is the definition of a warp rib. If the picks floated over two ends instead, it would be a weft rib.

questions.q: A designer wants a looser, flatter cloth from the same yarns and sett as an existing plain weave. Which weave gives that directly?
questions.explain: The lecture describes 2/2 hopsack as a looser, flatter cloth because pairs of threads interlace as one. Warp rib is corded rather than flat.

questions.q: At the same sett and yarns, a 3/3 hopsack is firmer than a 2/2 hopsack.
questions.explain: Longer floats mean fewer interlacings, so the 3/3 hopsack is looser, not firmer. Firmness falls as the group size grows.

questions.q: An upholstery buyer wants the boldest, most open basket texture. Which of these weaves gives it?
questions.explain: The 3/3 hopsack has the longest floats and largest groups of the options, so its basket texture is the boldest. Plain weave has no basket effect at all.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: A harder mix across the lecture: spotting false statements, two-step reasoning and the mistakes students most often make.

questions.q: Which statement about a 2/2 warp rib is FALSE?
options: Each end lifts for two picks and sinks for two
It can be woven on two healds
Each pick floats over two ends
questions.explain: In a warp rib the picks interlace singly; it is the ends that float over two picks. The other three statements are all taken from the lecture.

questions.q: A 3/3 hopsack is drawn on point paper 36 ends wide and 36 picks high. How many squares are filled?
questions.explain: Each end is up for three picks in every six, i.e. half the time, so half of 36 × 36 = 1,296 squares are filled: 648.

questions.q: A student writes that a 2/2 hopsack repeats on 2 ends × 2 picks. What is the correct repeat and why?
options: 2 × 4, because the ends float over two picks
4 × 4, because both ends and picks work in pairs
4 × 2, because the picks float over two ends
questions.explain: A pair up and a pair down takes four ends, and likewise four picks, so the hopsack repeat is 4 × 4. The 2 × 2 repeat belongs to plain weave, which the student has confused with its derivative.

questions.q: A 2/2 weft rib is the same weave as a 2/2 warp rib turned through 90°.
questions.explain: Both extend plain weave by two in one direction only; swap the roles of ends and picks and one becomes the other. That is why the repeats are 2 × 4 and 4 × 2.

questions.q: In a 2/2 weft rib, which threads interlace exactly as they would in plain weave?
questions.explain: Each end still goes over one pick and under the next; only the picks float, over two ends at a time. In a warp rib it is the picks that keep the plain interlacing.

questions.q: Why can a 2/2 hopsack be woven on only two healds?
options: Because its repeat is only four picks
Because ends 1 and 2 move identically and ends 3 and 4 move identically but opposite
Because the weft does all the interlacing
questions.explain: Healds are counted by the number of different end movements. In a 2/2 hopsack there are only two movements, so two healds carry all the ends. Reversibility and repeat length have nothing to do with heald count.

questions.q: Treating the plain-weave equivalent as cover factor ÷ divisor, a panama woven at a cover factor of 21 corresponds to what plain-weave cover factor? Use the divisor 1.4 and give one decimal.
questions.explain: 21 ÷ 1.4 = 15.0, so the panama at 21 is only as firm as a plain weave at 15.

questions.q: In the fancy basket 3-2 all the groups of threads are of equal size.
questions.explain: The whole point of the fancy basket is that the groups are unequal — three threads then two — which produces its irregular look.

questions.q: A warp rib is woven at the same sett as a plain weave in the same yarns and the weft shows through between the cords. What does the lecture's reasoning suggest?
options: The sett should be raised, because ribs interlace less often than plain weave
questions.explain: Ribs and hopsacks need a higher sett than plain weave to look firm; at plain-weave sett the cover is insufficient. A finer warp or fewer picks would open the cloth even more.

questions.q: Which of these weaves gives the highest warp crimp with the same yarns and sett?
questions.explain: The warp in a warp rib bends over pairs of picks, so its take-up is the highest; in a weft rib the warp lies straightest. The lecture points to Weaving Calculations 15 for the crimp figures.
